Empirical Research Plan  
“Birth Order, Son Preference and Child Height in India (NFHS)”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred design:  Sibling-fixed-effects (family FE) panel combined with an instrumental-variable (IV) for endogenous birth-order/ family size.

Why this design?  
• Height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) are determined by resources, parental preferences and genetics.  Family FE purge all time-invariant parental and household factors (wealth, caste, long-run nutrition, genetics).  
• Birth order is NOT exogenous because parents decide whether to have another child.  In a setting with strong son preference, the decision to continue child-bearing depends on the sex of previous births.  
• Child sex at conception is biologically random (conditional on no prenatal sex selection).  Hence the sex composition of older siblings is an exogenous shock that shifts the probability the focal child is later-born.  We instrument BirthOrder (and the interaction BirthOrder × Girl) with indicators for “all older siblings are girls.”  This follows the classic Angrist–Evans (1998) family-size IV logic but adapted to a gender-preference setting.  

Equations:  
First stage  BirthOrder_ij = π0 + π1 AllOlderGirls_ij + … + θ_j + η_ij  
Second stage  HAZ_ij = β1 Girl_ij + β2 BirthOrder^ IV_ij + β3 Girl_ij × BirthOrder^ IV_ij + X_ij + θ_j + ε_ij  

θ_j = family (mother) fixed effect.  
β3 is the causal “extra” height penalty for girls that comes only from differential treatment given birth-order.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable(s)  
T1: BirthOrder_ij  = child’s parity (2,3,4…).  
T2: Girl_ij × BirthOrder_ij – captures son-preference-driven differential treatment.

Instrument  
Z_ij = 1 if all older siblings of child i in family j are girls (or, for the 2nd-born, indicator that 1st-born is a girl).  

Control group (counterfactual)  
• Within the same family: the sibling(s) of different birth order/sex serve as controls.  
• Between families: families where older siblings include at least one boy, thus having weaker incentive to keep having children.

Key variation  
Cross-sectional within family at a point in time – no explicit “timing.”  Identification uses quasi-random assignment of older-sibling sex to generate exogenous variation in whether the focal child is high-parity and whether she grows up in a boy-scarce household.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Sex of each birth is random conditional on covariates (no selective abortion up to that birth).  
Plausibility: Reasonable for births before widespread ultrasound (early 1990s) and for 1st births even later.  We will test balance and run robustness restricting to older cohorts/pre-1995.

A2. “Exclusion” for IV: older-sibling sex affects height only through (i) shifting birth order / family size or (ii) altering parental son preference via sibling composition.  
Plausibility: Main alternative pathway is psychological spillovers (e.g., competition) – mitigated by family FE; we will include sibship-size controls to separate the two channels.

A3. Stable unit treatment value within family conditional on FE (no cross-child externalities that differ by instrument aside from treatment).  
Plausibility: Possible resource competition, but those are part of the treatment we wish to capture.

A4. Monotonicity: families with “all girls” do not decide to stop earlier because of the instrument (reasonable under son preference).

A5. No differential measurement error correlated with instrument.  NFHS uses standardized anthropometry, plausibly satisfied.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Prenatal sex selection breaks randomness of the instrument after ultrasound diffusion.  
Fix:  (a) Restrict to births before 1995; (b) show results by cohort and by high- vs low-ultrasound states; (c) use sex ratio tests (conditional on covariates) to verify randomness.

Threat 2: Selective survival – stunted girls may have higher mortality, leaving a positively selected sample.  
Fix:  (a) Include only children <5 where mortality bias is smaller; (b) use inverse-probability weights based on sibling mortality; (c) show bounds (Lee 2009 trimming).

Threat 3: “Exclusion” violated because older-sibling sex could influence height through sibling competition rather than via birth order.  
Fix:  Include sibship size and composition controls; show that IV estimates are robust to adding current family size; present placebo test on prenatal outcomes (birth weight) that should not respond to postnatal investment.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # fast FE + IV regressions
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov
library(lmtest)         # coeftest

# 1. Load & merge NFHS rounds -------------------------------------------
files <- list.files("data_nfhs/", pattern = "*.csv", full.names = TRUE)
nfhs  <- rbindlist(lapply(files, fread), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------
# keep children 0–59 months with valid anthropometry
nfhs <- nfhs[age_months <= 59 & !is.na(haz)]

# family (mother) identifier
nfhs[, family_id := paste0(hhid, "_", mother_line_no)]

# birth order within mother
setorder(nfhs, family_id, dob)
nfhs[, birth_order := seq_len(.N), by = family_id]

# girl dummy
nfhs[, girl := as.integer(sex == "Female")]

# instrument: all older siblings are girls
nfhs[, older_sibs := birth_order - 1]
nfhs[, older_girls := ifelse(older_sibs == 0, 0,
                             sum(sex == "Female") - girl), by = family_id]
nfhs[, all_older_girls := as.integer(older_sibs > 0 & older_girls == older_sibs)]

# covariates
nfhs[, X := .(age_months, age_months^2, wealth_quintile, urban,
              mother_education, state, survey_round)]

# 3. Main specification ---------------------------------------------------
# IV with family FE
iv_form <- haz ~ girl + birth_order + girl:birth_order + age_months + I(age_months^2) |
                   girl + (birth_order + girl:birth_order ~ all_older_girls)

mod_main <- feols(iv_form,
                  data = nfhs,
                  cluster = ~family_id,
                  fixef = ~family_id)

summary(mod_main, cluster = "family_id")

# 4. Robustness: restrict to pre-1995 births -----------------------------
nfhs_pre95 <- nfhs[year_of_birth < 1995]
mod_rb <- feols(iv_form,
                data = nfhs_pre95,
                cluster = ~family_id,
                fixef = ~family_id)
summary(mod_rb, cluster = "family_id")
```

(Additional checks: add sibship-size controls, run placebo on birth weight, conduct Hausman test against OLS-FE.)

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory and prior descriptive work predict:

• Birth-order effect: later-born children grow shorter (resource dilution). β2 < 0, roughly −0.05 to −0.10 HAZ per additional birth.  
• Son preference interaction: girls suffer an additional penalty when they are higher parity and when all older siblings are girls (strongest competition for resources).  β3 < 0, magnitude around −0.10 to −0.15 HAZ for 3rd-born girls relative to 3rd-born boys.  
Combined, a 3rd-born girl with only older sisters might be ~0.25–0.30 sd shorter than a 1st-born boy in the same family.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist (Self-Assessment)
------------------------------------------------------------
1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = some concern, 0 = weak.

1. Randomness / relevance of instrument……………… 0.7  
2. Exclusion restriction……………………………………… 0.6  
3. Correct functional form / FE adequacy……………… 0.8  
4. No selective attrition / survival bias………………… 0.6  
5. Robust standard errors & multiple checks………… 1.0  

Overall: 3.7 / 5.
